text: The merged New Hotspots universe should prioritize bottlenecks created by AI infrastructure moving from accelerator availability toward power, interconnection, high-voltage equipment, firm generation, HBM, advanced packaging, cooling and permitting constraints.

Large-load interconnection and data-center tariff design are top-ranked chokepoint nodes because they determine whether hyperscaler demand converts into energized load, utility capex and supplier orders.

High-voltage transformers, switchgear, grid equipment, cables and EPC execution capacity should be treated as a combined grid-equipment chokepoint rather than separate generic electrical-equipment stories.
HBM and advanced packaging remain live AI compute bottlenecks, but Layer 2 must separate demand-side mega caps from scarcer supplier nodes and check whether pricing already discounts the shortage.
Firm power and nuclear-related names should be decomposed into operating nuclear generation, advanced reactor licensing, fuel availability, component suppliers, EPC capacity and grid integration.

The universe still needs dedicated Layer 1B expansions for liquid cooling, water/permitting constraints, Asian HBM/advanced-packaging suppliers, cable/transformer specialists and maritime logistics chokepoints.

Before any higher-conviction ranking, each candidate requires primary-source validation using filings, earnings calls, regulatory dockets, backlog disclosures, capex plans, customer evidence and market-pricing checks.

New Hotspots should be tracked as an AI power-access chain: hyperscaler demand -> utility interconnection -> tariff/cost allocation -> transmission upgrades -> transformers/switchgear/substations -> EPC execution -> on-site power/cooling.
Highest bottleneck score belongs to high-voltage transformers and switchgear because multiple 2026 sources identify electrical equipment shortages as project-timing constraints.
Large-load tariffs are not just policy noise; they are evidence filters that separate speculative megawatt requests from binding customer commitments.
AEP Ohio's binding data-center contract updates and future load-study tranches should be monitored as recurring catalysts for grid-access demand quality.
FERC/PJM co-location rulemaking and related tariff decisions are key catalysts for the nuclear/generation-adjacent data-center model.
Electrical OEM earnings should be tracked for orders, backlog, book-to-bill, capacity additions, transformer lead times, and data-center-specific order growth.
EPC company backlogs and utility transmission awards are the best evidence that tariff-approved load is becoming executable grid capex.
Need more project-level verification linking individual data-center campuses to named transformer, switchgear, substation, and EPC suppliers.
Need market-pricing layer in later funnel stage: many obvious beneficiaries may already reflect strong AI/grid demand in valuation; Layer 2A intentionally excludes valuation judgment.
Need region-by-region mapping for Virginia, Ohio, Texas, Indiana, Illinois, Oregon, Colorado, and Minnesota because tariff rules and grid bottlenecks are state/RTO specific.
AEP is the strongest regulated-utility mapping in this chunk because its Ohio tariff and binding data-center MW disclosures create unusually concrete evidence for AI-related large-load demand.
GEV is the strongest equipment-vendor mapping because cached evidence ties Q1 2026 data-center orders directly to Electrification equipment and grid/generation bottleneck nodes.
D is a key regulated-utility mapping for Virginia/PJM data-center load, but cost-allocation and transmission upgrade treatment must be checked in regulatory filings before upgrading conviction.
TLN is a high-beta policy-test mapping for nuclear co-location and data-center firm-power procurement; its relationship is highly dependent on FERC/PJM treatment of co-located load.
ETN and PWR are plausible bottleneck suppliers for electrical equipment and grid EPC execution, but the current chunk needs direct order, backlog, lead-time, and customer-exposure evidence.
CEG is a credible firm-power/nuclear PPA mapping, but without verified signed hyperscaler contracts and incremental economics it should remain an inference rather than a fact-level relationship.
EXC, NI, XEL, and POR broaden the regulated-utility map beyond AEP and Dominion, but each needs docket-level tariff, cost-allocation, and customer-commitment verification.

HUBB is a lower-evidence, potentially less-obvious component supplier mapping; upgrade only if utility T&D component backlog and data-center/grid-modernization demand are directly supported by filings or management disclosures.

Need direct company filing checks for ETN, PWR, CEG, EXC, NI, XEL, POR, and HUBB before any Layer 2 ranking: segment exposure, backlog, customer concentration, tariff terms, regulatory dockets, signed contracts, and capex recovery.

Need market-pricing checks for all tickers in this chunk, including recent relative performance, valuation expansion, earnings revisions, short interest, and whether the AI power-grid narrative is already crowded.
Need FERC/PJM status verification as of June 2026 for co-located data-center load, network upgrade charges, generator-adjacent structures, and impacts on TLN, CEG, D, EXC, and AEP.

Need supplier lead-time and capacity evidence for transformers, switchgear, breakers, capacitors, substations, and EPC labor to separate true chokepoint beneficiaries from broad AI-infrastructure sympathy names.

Within this candidate chunk, direct chokepoint exposure ranks strongest for MU, SSNLF, 000660.KS, VRT, AVGO, and MRVL because they map to HBM/memory, data-center physical infrastructure, custom AI silicon, AI networking, and optical/data-movement nodes.

NVDA and AMD are core AI compute demand drivers and create pull-through for HBM, packaging, power, and cooling, but they should be treated as visible demand-driver nodes rather than under-discovered bottleneck candidates without a market-pricing check.

MTZ, ITRI, and NEE are derivative power-grid beneficiaries: the thesis depends on whether large-load data-center demand converts into signed utility capex, PPAs, interconnection upgrades, grid-edge contracts, or executable backlog.

MTZ requires project-level evidence tying Power Delivery or Clean Energy backlog to data-center interconnection, substation, or transmission work; current evidence shows backlog and segment exposure but not data-center-specific causality.

ITRI requires customer/order evidence proving that utilities are buying grid-edge intelligence or demand-response tools specifically because of large-load/data-center growth rather than general AMI and resiliency spending.

SMCI requires elevated verification because its relationship to the theme is operationally direct but vulnerable to margin compression, accounting quality, customer concentration, inventory risk, and platform-qualification risk.

For all HBM names, the next critical evidence is not just roadmap announcements but qualified volume shipments, customer allocation, yield, packaging capacity, pricing duration, and whether non-HBM DRAM tightness persists.

For AVGO and MRVL, the key diligence path is to separate AI networking, custom silicon, and optical/interconnect revenue from broader semiconductor or software revenue, then test customer concentration and duration of design wins.

TSM should remain the anchor mapping for the advanced-packaging/foundry node; relationship is high-quality but needs market-pricing and capacity-allocation checks because expectations are likely elevated.
ONTO's HBM metrology relationship upgraded from hypothesis to fact because the company disclosed a more than $240 million HBM manufacturer VPA through 2027.
CARR's cooling relationship upgraded because Q1 2026 evidence includes data-center orders up over 500% and 2026 sales coverage from backlog.
TT's cooling relationship strengthened by the LiquidStack acquisition; next layer should test whether liquid-cooling exposure is large enough to move consolidated revenue and margins.
COHR appears to have a more direct AI networking bottleneck relationship than LITE in this chunk due to explicit 800G/1.6T datacenter demand and capacity-expansion commentary.

AMAT, LRCX and KLAC need order-quality decomposition: AI/HBM/advanced-packaging exposure may be real, but total semicap revenue can also be driven by broader foundry, memory, China, and cyclic WFE factors.
FLEX and JCI remain diluted second-order mappings until data-center-specific revenue, backlog, customer concentration, and margin contribution are quantified.

Layer 2C should add market-pricing checks for all 12 names: relative performance since AI-power/cooling/CoWoS narrative acceleration, valuation expansion, estimate revisions, and short-interest changes.

FIX and EME are the strongest mechanical/electrical construction mappings in this chunk; both should be tracked through backlog/RPO mix, labor capacity, data-center customer concentration and margin conversion rather than treated as generic AI plays.
AMZN, MSFT, GOOGL and META are best used as demand-side validation and procurement-signal tickers for AI data centers, power, grid and nuclear, not as pure bottleneck suppliers.

BWXT, CCJ and LEU form the more credible nuclear supply-chain subgroup: BWXT for components/services/fuel, CCJ for uranium/conversion/Westinghouse, and LEU for HALEU/enrichment; all require separation of AI-driven demand from broader nuclear-cycle demand.

FLR needs direct project-level verification before ranking higher: confirm funded nuclear/power EPC awards, Fluor's economic exposure to NuScale, and any connection between power projects and hyperscaler or data-center load.
OKLO and NNE remain early-stage/speculative until licensing, fuel, financing, binding offtake, engineering validation and first deployment milestones are independently confirmed.

For this chunk, next Layer 2C checks should include market-pricing/crowding: relative performance, valuation expansion, earnings revision dependence, short interest and whether AI power narratives are already embedded.
ORCL should be treated as a demand validator and capacity builder, not a direct supply-chain chokepoint; monitor RPO conversion, lease commitments, capex and power-secured data-center capacity.

EQIX and DLR are data-center capacity/interconnection mappings where scarcity depends on power-ready sites, liquid-cooling capability and interconnection availability rather than generic square footage.

STX and WDC have stronger-than-initial Layer 1 evidence as secondary AI infrastructure chokepoints because nearline HDD capacity appears tight and AI/cloud workloads increase exabyte-scale storage needs.

CAT and CMI have direct evidence of data-center-driven power-generation demand; they should be grouped with backup/bridge power and large-engine/generator bottlenecks rather than generic industrial machinery.
GNRC has plausible C&I generator and packaging exposure to data centers, but needs direct order, backlog and customer evidence before being ranked with CAT/CMI.

ENPH relevance improved after announcing an AI-data-center solid-state-transformer platform, but evidence remains early-stage product-option evidence without orders, certification or customer validation.

FSLR maps to hyperscaler clean-power procurement and domestic solar supply, but intermittency means it is not a firm-power chokepoint unless tied to storage, grid interconnection or contracted data-center PPAs.
SBAC should remain deprioritized for this theme unless filings reveal measurable edge-compute, AI workload, private wireless or data-center-adjacent revenue.

Need entity-status verification for NEP/XPLR and asset-level proof that any renewable PPAs or infrastructure assets are directly tied to AI data-center loads; parent NEE evidence should not be automatically assigned to NEP.
Market-pricing checks remain missing for this chunk: relative performance, valuation expansion, earnings revisions, short interest and whether AI-power/storage narratives are already crowded.

WCC belongs in the distributor/integrator bucket for data-center electrical, communications, utility and grid services exposure; evidence is strong for revenue/backlog growth, but bottleneck control is weaker than OEMs because it distributes and integrates rather than manufactures scarce equipment.

NVT maps to electrical connection/protection/enclosure systems for data centers and utilities; treat as a less-obvious component supplier with medium-high thematic relevance pending segment-purity validation.
WIRE should be removed from active public ticker universe; Encore Wire is now part of Prysmian after the July 2, 2024 acquisition and no longer has listed shares.
PRYMY/PRY maps to high-voltage transmission, power grid, North America construction cable and data-center fiber/power cabling; Prysmian also absorbs former Encore Wire exposure.
NEX.PA maps to electrification, PWR-Transmission, PWR-Grid and North American low/medium-voltage cable expansion, with Q1 2026 evidence of data-center activity and €7.9B PWR-Transmission backlog.
SIEGY maps to Smart Infrastructure electrification/electrical products and automation; data-center relationship is current and factual, but conglomerate dilution requires purity adjustment.
SBGSY maps strongly to data-center energy management and power distribution; highest relationship quality in this chunk, but requires valuation-crowding and expectations checks.
ABBNY maps to electrification, automation and data-center/grid demand; relationship is factual but lower-purity than Schneider because ABB spans multiple end markets and product categories.

Layer 2C should add market-pricing checks for WCC, NVT, PRYMY/PRY, NEX.PA, SIEGY, SBGSY and ABBNY: relative performance since AI-power-chain narrative emerged, forward multiples, revisions, short interest and order/backlog expectations.
Need primary filings or transcripts for each ticker to quantify data-center exposure by segment; current evidence often confirms direction but not exact revenue purity or margin contribution.
